claim: The mammalian epidermis has two main physical barriers: an air-liquid interface barrier formed by the stratum corneum (SC) and a liquid-liquid interface barrier formed by tight junctions (TJs).
source: The mammalian epidermis has two main physical barriers, an air-liquid interface barrier formed by the stratum corneum (SC) and a liquid-liquid interface barrier formed by tight junctions (TJs) (Kubo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kubo et al., 2012, indicating prior published work.

claim: The TJ barrier of the epidermis consists of only a single layer of TJs forming a honeycomb-like mesh in the SG2 layer.
source: Despite its critical importance for the skin homeostasis, the TJ barrier of the epidermis consists of only a single layer of TJs forming a honeycomb-like mesh (TJ honeycomb) in the SG2 layer (Figure 1A) (Furuse et al., 2002; Kubo et al., 2009; Yoshida et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies (Furuse et al., 2002; Kubo et al., 2009; Yoshida et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: A significant number of TJ polygons in the TJ honeycomb of murine ear epidermis were double-edged (9.8 ± 0.6%).
source: We noticed that a significant number of TJ polygons in the TJ honeycomb of murine ear epidermis were double-edged (9.8 ± 0.6%, mean ± SEM, five independent assays; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from five independent assays and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The outer polygons were larger (1044.3 ± 20.6 µm2) than their adjacent single-edged polygons (905.8 ± 12.6 µm2).
source: The outer polygons were larger (1044.3 ± 20.6 µm2, mean ± SEM, n = 23), and the inner ones smaller (814.7 ± 15.7 µm2, n = 23), than their adjacent single-edged polygons (905.8 ± 12.6 µm2, n = 66; Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from microscopy data presented in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inner (smaller) polygon was located lower in the epidermis than the outer (larger) one in each double-edged polygon.
source: The inner (smaller) polygon was located lower in the epidermis than the outer (larger) one in each double-edged polygon (n = 99; Figure 1D and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D imaging data from 99 double-edged polygons shown in Figure 1D and Video 1.

claim: The outer polygon was located significantly higher (0.294 ± 0.024 µm) than the adjacent single-edged polygons (−0.076 ± 0.009 µm).
source: Furthermore, comparison of the average Z-axis position of the vertices of the polygons revealed that the outer polygon was located significantly higher (0.294 ± 0.024 µm, n = 55), and the inner one significantly lower (−0.751 ± 0.036 µm, n = 55), than the adjacent single-edged polygons (−0.076 ± 0.009 µm, n = 55; Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative Z-axis position measurements presented in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A new smaller (interior) polygon appeared beneath a pre-existing (exterior) polygon, forming a double-edged polygon, followed by disappearance of the exterior polygon.
source: Namely, a new smaller (interior) polygon appeared beneath a pre-existing (exterior) polygon, forming a double-edged polygon as observed in the fixed samples (Figure 1D), followed by disappearance of the exterior polygon (Figure 1F and Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo live imaging data shown in Figure 1F and Video 4.

claim: Replacement of the old exterior polygon by a new interior polygon resulted in natural translocation of the cell body from the inside to the outside of the TJ barrier.
source: Replacement of the old exterior polygon by a new interior polygon resulted in natural translocation of the cell body placed between the two polygons from the inside to the outside of the TJ barrier (discussed below in the cell turnover model, Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed dynamics of TJ polygon replacement and is discussed in relation to Figure 4B.

claim: The interior TJ polygons exhibited barrier function that protected the extracellular portion of Dsg1 against ETA.
source: The interior TJ polygons exhibited barrier function that protected the extracellular portion of Dsg1 against ETA (representative images, Figure 2A–C and Video 5; quantitative data of double-edged polygons [1.689 ± 0.020 times, mean ± SEM, n = 149] and their adjacent single-edged polygons [0.810 ± 0.006 times, n = 736], Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by permeation assay data shown in Figure 2A–C, Video 5, and quantitative analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: Claudin-1 was localized to both the exterior and interior polygons.
source: Claudin-1, a major transmembrane protein of epidermal TJ (Furuse et al., 2002), was localized to both the exterior and interior polygons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Furuse et al., 2002.

claim: tTJ-specific proteins (angulin-1 and tricellulin) were localized on all edges of the interior polygons of the double-edged ZO-1-positive polygons, while the exterior polygons were bTJs.
source: In stratified epithelia of the epidermis, we observed the localization of tTJ-specific proteins (angulin-1 and tricellulin) on all edges of the interior polygons of the double-edged ZO-1-positive polygons, while the exterior polygons were bTJs (Figure 2B,E and Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 2B, E and Video 6.

claim: The interior TJ polygons consist of tTJs formed among three SG2 cells: two vertically aligned SG2 cells and a laterally adjacent SG2 cell.
source: The interior TJ polygon consists of tTJs formed among three SG2 cells: two vertically aligned SG2 cells and a laterally adjacent SG2 cell (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on the observed localization of tTJ proteins and the 3D structure shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The basic shape of TJ-bearing SG2 cells is a flattened Kelvin's tetrakaidecahedron (f-TKD).
source: We thus concluded that the basic shape of SG2 cells is f-TKD.
evidence: This conclusion is based on 3D imaging of isolated SG2 cells shown in Figure 3F and Video 7.

claim: The TJ-bearing SG2 cells have an f-TKD–like polyhedral shape, with TJs on their edges.
source: The immunofluorescent staining of isolated SG2 cells and their 3D rendered images demonstrated that the TJ-bearing SG2 cells have an f-TKD–like polyhedral shape, with TJs on their edges (Figure 3F and Video 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and 3D rendering data shown in Figure 3F and Video 7.

claim: The murine ear epidermis consists of a basal layer, a spinous layer, and three layers of SG cells, and exhibits a regular structure of vertically aligned SC cells (corneocytes) and SG cells.
source: The murine ear epidermis consists of a basal layer, a spinous layer, and three layers of SG cells, and exhibits a regular structure of vertically aligned SC cells (corneocytes) and SG cells (Mackenzie, 1969; 1975; Kubo et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Mackenzie, 1969; 1975; Kubo et al., 2009).

claim: During the course of its upward movement, a keratinocyte becomes flattened at the SG, forms TJs with adjacent cells in the SG2 layer, loses its TJs in the SG1 layer and is finally cornified to form the SC.
source: During the course of its upward movement, a keratinocyte becomes flattened at the SG, forms TJs with adjacent cells in the SG2 layer (the second cell layer of the SG), loses its TJs in the SG1 layer (the top layer of the SG) and is finally cornified to form the SC (Figure 1A) (Kubo et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Kubo et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The TJ is a specialized intercellular adhesion complex that is crucial for epidermal barrier function, as it seals the paracellular space of epithelial cellular sheets.
source: The TJ is a specialized intercellular adhesion complex that is crucial for epidermal barrier function, as it seals the paracellular space of epithelial cellular sheets (Tsukita et al., 2001; Van Itallie and Anderson, 2014; Krug et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Tsukita et al., 2001; Van Itallie and Anderson, 2014; Krug et al., 2014).

claim: Maintenance of the TJ barrier is crucial for proper formation of the SC.
source: Maintenance of the TJ barrier is crucial for proper formation of the SC (Sugawara et al., 2013), and thus for maintaining the physical barriers of the skin.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sugawara et al., 2013.

claim: Epidermal barrier dysfunctions cause not only lethal congenital disorders, but also a predisposition to the development of allergic diseases.
source: Epidermal barrier dysfunctions cause not only lethal congenital disorders, but also a predisposition to the development of allergic diseases (McGrath and Uitto, 2008; Akiyama, 2010; Kubo et al., 2012; Weidinger and Novak, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies (McGrath and Uitto, 2008; Akiyama, 2010; Kubo et al., 2012; Weidinger and Novak, 2015).

claim: The epidermis consists of keratinocytes that proliferate only in the basal layer and move upward to sequentially form stratum spinosum, stratum granulosum (SG), and SC, and finally shed off from the top layer of the SC.
source: The epidermis consists of keratinocytes that proliferate only in the basal layer and move upward to sequentially form stratum spinosum, stratum granulosum (SG), and SC, and finally shed off from the top layer of the SC (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of epidermal structure and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The double-edged polygons are where cells translocate across the TJ barrier and thus are the key structures for barrier homeostasis.
source: These findings indicate that the double-edged polygons are where cells translocate across the TJ barrier and thus are the key structures for barrier homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed dynamics of TJ polygon replacement.

claim: The development of the occlusive paracellular barrier of the interior TJ polygons prevents barrier leakage during cellular translocation from inside to outside the TJ barrier.
source: These observations indicate that the development of the occlusive paracellular barrier of the interior TJ polygons prevents barrier leakage during cellular translocation from inside to outside the TJ barrier (discussed below in Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed barrier function of interior polygons shown in Figure 2 and discussed in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The f-TKD model provides a coherent mechanistic explanation of how the regular stacks of corneocytes are constructed.
source: The f-TKD model thus provides a coherent mechanistic explanation of how the regular stacks of corneocytes are constructed.
evidence: This claim is based on the computational model's ability to reproduce the observed interdigitation pattern.

claim: The regular columnar stack of flattened corneocytes in murine ear epidermis demonstrates a regular zig-zag interdigitation pattern between two adjacent cell columns.
source: The regular columnar stack of flattened corneocytes in murine ear epidermis demonstrates a regular zig-zag interdigitation pattern between two adjacent cell columns (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 reproduced from Figure 1 of Mackenzie [1975]) (Mackenzie, 1969; Christophers, 1972; Menton, 1976; Ball, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Mackenzie, 1969; 1975; Christophers, 1972; Menton, 1976; Ball, 2001) and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The regular interdigitation pattern was spontaneously reproduced by the f-TKD model.
source: This regular interdigitation pattern was spontaneously reproduced by our f-TKD model (Figure 6A), in which cell differentiation in the SG2 cell layer occurs in turn in pairs of adjacent cell columns.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational simulation results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The f-TKD model suggests that homeostasis of the SC–SG layers is maintained by the spatiotemporal orchestration of cell differentiation in the SG2 cell layer, rather than by the kinetics of stem cell proliferation and differentiation in the basal layer.
source: The f-TKD model further suggests that homeostasis of the SC–SG layers is maintained by the spatiotemporal orchestration of cell differentiation in the SG2 cell layer, rather than by the kinetics of stem cell proliferation and differentiation in the basal layer.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the f-TKD model's predictions.

claim: The f-TKD model is consistent with a pioneering computational simulation suggesting that the regular 3D stacking structure of the SC can be spontaneously formed by randomly supplied cells.
source: Our model is consistent with a pioneering computational simulation suggesting that the regular 3D stacking structure of the SC can be spontaneously formed by randomly supplied cells (Honda et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Honda et al., 1996.

claim: The f-TKD model accords with in vivo cell-tracing studies demonstrating a random supply of cells from the spinous layer to the SG layer.
source: Our model also accords with in vivo cell-tracing studies demonstrating a random supply of cells from the spinous layer to the SG layer (Doupé et al., 2010), and in vivo live observations of the upward movement of spinous layer cells funneling into preexisting cell columns of the SG (Rompolas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Doupé et al., 2010; Rompolas et al., 2016).

claim: In the f-TKD model, the cell columns exist only in the SG and SC layers, rather than extending from the basal layer through to the SC.
source: In our f-TKD model, the cell columns exist only in the SG and SC layers, rather than extending from the basal layer through to the SC.
evidence: This is a key feature of the proposed f-TKD model.

claim: Once the cells enter the SG layer, cell turnover in adjacent columns is tightly coordinated in a spatiotemporal manner, leading to the regular interdigitation pattern.
source: Once the cells enter the SG layer, cell turnover in adjacent columns is tightly coordinated in a spatiotemporal manner, leading to the regular interdigitation pattern (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is based on the f-TKD model and illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: If all the keratinocytes in the epidermis formed TJs, cells located in the upper epidermis would likely starve due to their segregation from the nutrient supply by multi-layered TJ barriers.
source: If all the keratinocytes in the epidermis formed TJs, cells located in the upper epidermis would likely starve due to their segregation from the nutrient supply by multi-layered TJ barriers.
evidence: This is a speculative reasoning about the biological necessity of single-layered TJ barriers.

claim: It is biologically reasonable that the TJ barrier is single-layered in stratified epithelia.
source: Therefore, it is biologically reasonable that the TJ barrier is single-layered in stratified epithelia (Kubo et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Kubo et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2013) and biological reasoning.

claim: TJ formation is restricted only between SG2 cells.
source: Our observations revealed that TJ formation is restricted only between SG2 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Various mammalian epidermis shows a regular interdigitation pattern in the SC.
source: Various mammalian epidermis shows a regular interdigitation pattern in the SC (Christophers, 1972; Mackenzie et al., 1981), suggesting that the f-TKD cell turnover mechanism governs cell differentiation in mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Christophers, 1972; Mackenzie et al., 1981).

claim: The f-TKD cell turnover mechanism governs cell differentiation in mammals.
source: Various mammalian epidermis shows a regular interdigitation pattern in the SC (Christophers, 1972; Mackenzie et al., 1981), suggesting that the f-TKD cell turnover mechanism governs cell differentiation in mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of regular interdigitation patterns across mammalian species.

claim: The basic concept of the spatiotemporal orchestration of SG cell differentiation in the f-TKD model would be sufficient to explain the regular interdigitation pattern of corneocytes observed in various types of cornified skin.
source: Nonetheless, the basic concept of the spatiotemporal orchestration of SG cell differentiation in the f-TKD model would be sufficient to explain the regular interdigitation pattern of corneocytes observed in various types of cornified skin (Mackenzie et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the model and supported by a citation to Mackenzie et al., 1981.

claim: The f-TKD cell turnover model of the SG provides a fundamental basis for the maintenance of barrier homeostasis during cell turnover in cornified stratified epithelia.
source: The f-TKD cell turnover model of the SG can be applied to stratified stacks of variously shaped polyhedral cells and provides a fundamental basis for the maintenance of barrier homeostasis during cell turnover in cornified stratified epithelia.
evidence: This is a concluding inference based on the entire study.

claim: Computational simulation of the in silico model reproduced the entire sequence of TJ replacement on f-TKD cells, including formation of TJs, transition of the f-TKD cells, and upward movement of differentiated keratinocytes as a stratified cell sheet.
source: Computational simulation of the in silico model (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Videos 9 and 10) reproduced the entire sequence of TJ replacement on f-TKD cells, including formation of TJs, transition of the f-TKD cells, and upward movement of differentiated keratinocytes as a stratified cell sheet, while maintaining the relative location of individual f-TKD cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Videos 9 and 10.

claim: The computational simulation confirmed the maintenance of TJ barrier homeostasis, cell-cell adhesion, and the physical strength of the cell sheet during cell turnover.
source: It therefore confirmed the maintenance of TJ barrier homeostasis, cell-cell adhesion, and the physical strength of the cell sheet during cell turnover.
evidence: This claim is based on the results of the computational simulation.

claim: The spatiotemporal regulation of dynamic TJ replacement and continuous cell turnover across the TJ honeycomb can be explained by three simple local rules governing the f-TKD cells.
source: The characteristic feature of the proposed f-TKD turnover model (Figure 5) is that the spatiotemporal regulation of dynamic TJ replacement and continuous cell turnover across the TJ honeycomb can be explained by the following three simple local rules governing the f-TKD cells: (1) bTJs are formed between two SG2 cells, and tTJs are formed at the tricellular cell contact among three SG2 cells; (2) An SG2 cell located higher than its six adjacent SG2 cells differentiates to become an SG1 cell; (3) The differentiation of a SG3 cell to become a SG2 cell is synchronized with the differentiation of the pre-existing SG2 cell to become a SG1 cell in each cell column (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on the proposed model and illustrated in Figures 4B and 5.

claim: The precise order for formation of the functional TJs, whereby the interior TJ polygon gains barrier function before the exterior TJ polygon disappears, is critical for TJ barrier homeostasis while cells are turned over.
source: The precise order for formation of the functional TJs, whereby the interior TJ polygon gains barrier function before the exterior TJ polygon disappears (Figure 4C), is critical for TJ barrier homeostasis while cells are turned over.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed dynamics and is illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: The average time required for cell turnover from entering to exiting the SG2 layer is 24 hr.
source: The nominal values for the model parameters were determined so that the simulated dynamics reproduce the experimentally observed ratio of double-edged polygons among all the polygons (9.8 ± 0.6%, Figure 1B), as well as the average time required for cell turnover from entering to exiting the SG2 layer (24 hr), estimated from the average cell turnover rate in mouse ear epidermis (Potten, 1975).
evidence: This claim is based on an estimate from the average cell turnover rate cited from Potten, 1975.

claim: A flattened variation of Kelvin's tetrakaidecahedron (f-TKD) shape was once observed in the corneocytes at the surface of murine ear skin in scanning electron microscopic studies.
source: A flattened variation of Kelvin's tetrakaidecahedron (f-TKD) shape (Figure 3C) was once observed in the corneocytes at the surface of murine ear skin in scanning electron microscopic studies (Allen and Potten, 1976; Menton, 1976) but has been overlooked for several decades.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Allen and Potten, 1976; Menton, 1976).

claim: Kelvin's tetrakaidecahedron was originally proposed by Lord Kelvin in 1887 as the optimal natural space-filling shape with minimal surface area.
source: Our in vivo observations can be coherently explained if we assume the SG cells have the shape of the Kelvin's tetrakaidecahedron, which was originally proposed by Lord Kelvin in 1887 as the optimal natural space-filling shape with minimal surface area (Figure 3B) (Thomson, 1887).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thomson, 1887.

claim: In simple epithelia, most TJs are formed as conventional bicellular TJs (bTJs) on the apical edges between two cells, and tricellular TJs (tTJs) are formed at tricellular contacts among three cells.
source: In simple epithelia, most TJs are formed as conventional bicellular TJs (bTJs) on the apical edges between two cells, and tricellular TJs (tTJs) are formed at tricellular contacts among three cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B) (Furuse et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Furuse et al., 2014 and illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Previous biotin permeation assays evaluated in vertical sections of mouse ear skin have not demonstrated barrier leakage at any TJ.
source: Previous biotin permeation assays evaluated in vertical sections of mouse ear skin have not demonstrated barrier leakage at any TJ (Furuse et al., 2002; Kubo et al., 2009), suggesting that the barrier homeostasis of TJs is maintained even while the TJ polygons are being replaced.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Furuse et al., 2002; Kubo et al., 2009).

claim: The barrier homeostasis of TJs is maintained even while the TJ polygons are being replaced.
source: Previous biotin permeation assays evaluated in vertical sections of mouse ear skin have not demonstrated barrier leakage at any TJ (Furuse et al., 2002; Kubo et al., 2009), suggesting that the barrier homeostasis of TJs is maintained even while the TJ polygons are being replaced.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of observed barrier leakage in prior studies.

claim: Epidermal homeostasis is maintained by balancing cell proliferation in the basal layer, cell translocation (differentiation) from the basal to the spinous layer, cell integration to the SC/SG layer, and cell shedding from the top of the SC as squames.
source: Epidermal homeostasis is maintained by balancing cell proliferation in the basal layer, cell translocation (differentiation) from the basal to the spinous layer, cell integration to the SC/SG layer, and cell shedding from the top of the SC as squames.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall understanding of epidermal homeostasis.

claim: Nutrients for stratified cells are mostly supplied from the basal connective tissue via diffusion through paracellular pathways.
source: Nutrients for stratified cells are mostly supplied from the basal connective tissue via diffusion through paracellular pathways.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of nutrient supply in stratified epithelia.

claim: Other mechanisms could be involved in maintaining TJ barrier homeostasis in simple epithelia and non-cornified stratified epithelia, where apoptotic cells are extruded to the outside TJ barrier by adjacent cells that migrate into the basal side of the apoptotic cells and form multi-junctional TJs.
source: Other mechanisms could be involved in maintaining TJ barrier homeostasis in simple epithelia and non-cornified stratified epithelia, where apoptotic cells are extruded to the outside TJ barrier by adjacent cells that migrate into the basal side of the apoptotic cells and form multi-junctional TJs (Pentecost et al., 2006; Eisenhoffer and Rosenblatt, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Pentecost et al., 2006; Eisenhoffer and Rosenblatt, 2011).

claim: The actual structure of the optimal space-filling shape with minimal surface area could be more complex than Kelvin's model.
source: The actual structure of the optimal space-filling shape with minimal surface area could be more complex than Kelvin's model (Lewis, 1943; Williams, 1968; Weaire and Phelan, 1994), and the shape and alignment of corneocytes are much more variegated in human skin compared to mouse ear skin (Mackenzie et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Lewis, 1943; Williams, 1968; Weaire and Phelan, 1994; Mackenzie et al., 1981).

claim: The shape and alignment of corneocytes are much more variegated in human skin compared to mouse ear skin.
source: The actual structure of the optimal space-filling shape with minimal surface area could be more complex than Kelvin's model (Lewis, 1943; Williams, 1968; Weaire and Phelan, 1994), and the shape and alignment of corneocytes are much more variegated in human skin compared to mouse ear skin (Mackenzie et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mackenzie et al., 1981.

claim: In the 1980s, the epidermal proliferative unit (EPU) concept postulated that each column of flattened corneocytes corresponds to a set of basal layer stem cells that proliferate directly under the column.
source: In the 1980s, the epidermal proliferative unit (EPU) concept postulated that each column of flattened corneocytes corresponds to a set of basal layer stem cells that proliferate directly under the column (Potten and Allen, 1975; Potten, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Potten and Allen, 1975; Potten, 2004).

claim: Recent in vivo cell-fate-tracing studies demonstrated more random cell fate decisions in the basal cell layer, with EPU model-like upward cell movement funneling into the cell columns of the SG, leading to a new concept: the epidermal differentiation unit (EDU).
source: However, recent in vivo cell-fate-tracing studies demonstrated more random cell fate decisions in the basal cell layer, with EPU model-like upward cell movement funneling into the cell columns of the SG, leading to a new concept: the epidermal differentiation unit (EDU) (Rompolas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rompolas et al., 2016.

claim: ZO-1-Venus transgenic mice were established using the involucrin promoter to drive expression of ZO-1 fused to Venus fluorescent protein.
source: To establish ZO-1-Venus transgenic mice, a transgenic vector was constructed with the involucrin promoter vector (pH3700-pL2 (Carroll and Taichman, 1992), kindly provided by Dr. Lorne Taichman), which contained the first involucrin intron, an SV40 intron, a β-galactosidase gene, and an SV40 polyadenylation site. Mouse cDNA encoding the full length of ZO-1 and Venus (Nagai et al., 2002) cDNA (kindly provided by Dr. Atsushi Miyawaki) was replaced with the β-galactosidase gene in the involucrin promoter vector.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used to generate the transgenic mice.

claim: Venus successfully labeled the TJs without any apparent change in their occlusive function.
source: Venus-positive junctions were observed to limit the inside-out permeation of the tracer (yellow arrows), indicating that Venus successfully labeled the TJs without any apparent change in their occlusive function.
evidence: This claim is supported by permeation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: No morphological changes were observed in the TJ honeycomb in ZO-1-Venus transgenic mice.
source: No morphological changes were observed in the TJ honeycomb in ZO-1-Venus transgenic mice.
evidence: This claim is based on observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Female 8- to 12-week-old C57B6/J mice were used as wild type in all experiments.
source: Female 8- to 12-week-old C57B6/J mice were used as wild type in all experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental animals used in the study.
